item.title: The Fold — 2026-11-10
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 10 November 2026: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang faces an FBI inquiry and shareholder lawsuit over a suspected Chinese spy, US tankers leave RAF Mildenhall amid Iran threats, Ukraine peace talks resume in Abu Dhabi, and M John Harrison wins the Booker Prize at 81.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday 10 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang faces an FBI investigation and a shareholder lawsuit over an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.
  • The US Air Force diverts refuelling tankers from RAF Mildenhall after an Iran-linked threat, even as Donald Trump calls fresh American strikes unlikely.
  • American, Russian and Ukrainian negotiators open their first substantive peace talks since February in Abu Dhabi to debate post-war European security.
  • Brazil’s Supreme Court closes its seven-year fake news inquiry while the Federal Police rewrite sensitivity reports on three justices and Banco Master.
  • Bank of England deputy governor Clare Lombardelli warns that Middle East energy shocks have pushed Britain into a low-gear job market for young workers.
  • M John Harrison wins the 2026 Booker Prize at the age of 81 for The End of Everything, becoming the award’s oldest laureate and its first from science fiction.

News

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang faces FBI probe and shareholder lawsuit over suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia and its co-founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, have been hit with a federal shareholder lawsuit in California alongside confirmation from the White House that the FBI is investigating his romantic relationship with a woman whom American intelligence officials believe to be an agent for China’s Ministry of State Security. Shares in the $4.3tn chipmaker fell by more than 4% on Monday, wiping roughly $190bn to $250bn from its market value in a single session. Five minutes after the closing bell, retail investors led by Mark Kistenmacher filed a complaint in San Jose federal court accusing Huang and the company of defrauding shareholders by concealing a personal entanglement that posed acute national security and commercial risks. (Guardian, BBC)

At the centre of the investigation is Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le and unrelated to the Nvidia chief, a former television reporter who became managing director at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based computing firm that rents access to graphics processors. Around the time the pair were photographed together at a Taipei bar in 2024, Megaspeed acquired $4.8bn worth of scarce Nvidia hardware in a sudden expansion that startled rivals. Over the weekend, Jensen Huang told employees in a memo that he had been unfaithful to his wife, while Nvidia’s board announced an independent inquiry into reports that he had been targeted by foreign intelligence. Nvidia maintains that neither corporate secrets nor American national security were compromised, and Beijing dismissed the allegations as groundless smears. (The Verge, BBC)

Speaking at a White House briefing on Monday after telephoning the executive, Donald Trump confirmed the FBI inquiry while defending Huang’s character and expressing sympathy for his family. Trump said he had asked Huang directly whether he knew the woman was a spy, accepted his denial, and expected him to emerge in good shape. Even so, the affair has raised uncomfortable questions for Washington: intelligence agencies reportedly briefed Trump roughly a year ago on the relationship, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a warning memo to senior officials ahead of the president’s trip to China in May. Because Nvidia supplies the frontier chips powering modern artificial intelligence and holds $99bn in equity across the sector, Huang has spent the past year pressing Trump to lift export bans on advanced H200 processors to China, arguing that AI advancement between the superpowers need not be a zero-sum contest. (The Verge, BBC, Guardian)

US evacuates tankers from RAF Mildenhall over Iran threat as war reshapes global emissions

The United States military evacuated aerial refuelling tankers from RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk on Monday and raised defensive alert levels across its East Anglian bases following intelligence of an Iran-linked threat. Two tankers inbound to Mildenhall diverted to Germany early on Monday before several more aircraft stationed at the base were flown out to Germany and other European airfields later in the day. American commanders simultaneously upgraded the security posture at RAF Mildenhall and nearby RAF Lakenheath to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the Pentagon’s second-highest threat level, indicating intelligence of a likely terrorist or sabotage action. The move comes weeks after Washington withdrew its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire after suspicious vans were seen near the perimeter in September, an incident that led counter-terrorism police to arrest eight men and that Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month had probably been coordinated from Tehran. (Guardian, BBC)

In Washington, however, Donald Trump struck a de-escalatory tone after Republicans suffered heavy midterm losses last week that senior figures, including Vice-President JD Vance, blamed in part on voter frustration over the nine-month Iran conflict. After meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani at the White House to discuss mediation, Trump declared Iran militarily finished and said fresh American strikes were highly unlikely, though US forces would maintain their naval blockade on Iranian ports. Brent crude slipped past $91.50 a barrel on Tuesday following his remarks. Meanwhile, scientists presenting the annual Global Carbon Budget at Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, reported that the war-driven oil and gas price surge has nudged global fossil fuel emissions down by 0.4% in 2026, with oil emissions falling by 2% and Chinese carbon output dipping by nearly 1% as drivers switch to electric vehicles and solar and wind capacity expands. Researchers cautioned that deforestation and south-east Asian wildfires still pushed total carbon dioxide emissions up from 42.8bn to 43.3bn tonnes, leaving less than four years of the world’s 1.5C carbon budget at current rates. (BBC, Guardian)

Abu Dhabi hosts first trilateral Ukraine peace talks since February amid European security nerves

Senior delegations from Washington, Kyiv and Moscow convened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their first substantive trilateral negotiations since February, with US officials pressing for a settlement as the war in Ukraine nears its fifth anniversary. Led on the American side by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the talks link territorial questions in eastern Ukraine—particularly control over Donetsk, where Moscow demands full Ukrainian withdrawal while Kyiv seeks a frozen contact line—to a proposal for a new post-war security architecture between Russia and Europe. US officials said both warring sides had privately shown slight flexibility on territory, and floated offering Ukraine a security guarantee modelled on Nato’s mutual-defence clause while reviving the Nato-Russia Council and lifting sanctions on Moscow. (Guardian, BBC)

European capitals greeted the blueprint with apprehension, fearing that a White House eager for a diplomatic prize after its midterm setback could entertain Vladimir Putin’s demand that Nato roll back its military footprint in eastern Europe. Envoys from Britain, France, Germany, Italy and the EU travelled to the United Arab Emirates to secure a seat at the table, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas noted that Europe already has a security architecture whose treaties Moscow has chosen to break. Elsewhere on Tuesday, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that anti-graft investigators under Operation Purgatory had detained Áron Orbán, the 49-year-old brother of former prime minister Viktor Orbán, alongside three others over an alleged visa-smuggling scheme at Hungary’s missions in Vietnam; in Jerusalem, more than 160 former Israeli security officials warned of far-right plots to disrupt the swearing-in of the new Knesset as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot moves to replace Benjamin Netanyahu’s ally Amir Ohana as speaker. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

England bans school phones from bags as Jemima Goldsmith speaks out after Russell Brand sentencing

Pupils across England will be barred from carrying mobile phones in their pockets or schoolbags from September 2027 under tightened statutory guidance announced by Education Secretary Lucy Powell. While rules introduced in June required schools to be phone-free throughout the day, many relied on policies allowing students to keep devices switched off in their bags; the updated framework instructs schools to use lockable pouches, secure lockers, morning collection points or site-wide bans. Headteachers’ unions welcomed the clarity on distraction but warned that providing magnetic pouches or secure storage for every pupil will require dedicated government funding as school leaders weigh early departure over reformed Ofsted inspections. (BBC, Guardian)

In the courts, the sentencing of former comedian Russell Brand to ten years and six months in prison for raping a fan and sexually assaulting three women between 2004 and 2009 prompted television producer Jemima Goldsmith to reveal that she had called police to remove him from her house during a violent incident in 2014. Goldsmith, who previously stayed silent to protect her teenage children, disclosed that she had assisted the journalists who exposed Brand in 2023 and promised to testify if the newspapers were sued. Meanwhile, British travellers face potential two-year Schengen bans and €10,000 fines because glitches in the European Union’s biometric Entry/Exit System have logged arrivals without recording departures; novelist Jojo Moyes was detained by border officers at Marseille and told her 90-day post-Brexit allowance had expired after the database failed to record her exit from Portugal in May, prompting Brussels to sue IBM and two European contractors. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

Brazil’s Supreme Court ends seven-year fake news inquiry as Federal Police rewrite Master reports

Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court has closed its fake news inquiry after 2,797 days, ending one of the most consequential proceedings in the country’s recent legal history. Acting on a request from Prosecutor-General Paulo Gonet, Chief Justice Edson Fachin signed a 31-page order on Monday archiving the probe, which was opened without a prosecutorial petition by then-chief justice Dias Toffoli in March 2019 and assigned without a draw to Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Across more than seven years and 12 deadline extensions, the inquiry served as the court’s central shield against digital militias and coup plots during Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency, generating roughly 1,600 criminal cases—including prosecutions from the 8 January 2023 uprising—while drawing criticism from jurists and the Bar Association for concentrating investigative and judicial powers in one magistrate. Fachin, who removed Moraes as rapporteur two months ago after Moraes sought to use the dossier to investigate fellow Justice André Mendonça, ruled that a preliminary inquiry cannot remain open indefinitely, though all past decisions and spin-off actions remain valid. (Folha, Folha)

The closure comes amid friction over ties between Supreme Court justices and Daniel Vorcaro, former controller of Banco Master. Federal Police leadership under director-general Andrei Rodrigues ordered officers on Monday to rewrite three reports requested by Fachin on interactions between Vorcaro and Justices Moraes, Toffoli and Kassio Nunes Marques, while removing commissioners Daniel Mostardeiro Cola and Wedson Cajé Lopes from their leadership posts in the anti-corruption and Supreme Court inquiries unit. Phone records showed Vorcaro flew to Brasília twice in November last year right before his arrest to meet Moraes and messaged him seeking delays to police operations before searching online for the Tremembé prison; police chiefs concluded the initial drafts contained analytical cross-referencing that could be viewed as an unauthorised probe of sitting justices, and ordered purely factual individual files by month’s end. Meanwhile, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva set three year-end priorities for Congress—a third phase of the Desenrola debt-forgiveness programme for micro-entrepreneurs, a provisional measure banning online betting, and big-tech regulation—while planning a cabinet reshuffle to return elected senators such as Rui Costa and Wellington Dias to the upper house to counter a 32-seat bolsonarista opposition bloc in 2027. (Folha, Meio, Folha, Meio)

Economy

Bank of England warns of ‘low-gear economy’ hitting young workers as December rate call stays live

Young people entering the British labour market are bearing the brunt of a recruitment freeze triggered by the nine-month war in Iran and higher business costs, Bank of England deputy governor Clare Lombardelli has warned. Speaking ahead of a London speech on Tuesday, the deputy governor for monetary policy described a low-gear economy defined by a low-hire, low-fire dynamic: employers are avoiding redundancies and retaining staff, but have paused recruitment while waiting to see whether energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty settle. That caution has pushed UK unemployment to 4.7% this year and lifted youth joblessness to its highest level outside the Covid pandemic since 2015, swelling the number of young people outside education, employment or training to nearly one million ahead of Alan Milburn’s review next week. (Guardian)

Lombardelli, who voted with the Monetary Policy Committee majority last week to lift the base rate from 3.75% to 4%—the first rate rise in three years—said December’s policy meeting remains live, with markets pricing even odds of another quarter-point increase. Across the Channel, Jens Eskelund, head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, warned officials in Brussels that with the bloc’s trade deficit with Beijing running at €1.18bn (£1bn) a day and Chinese exports forecast by Goldman Sachs to cut German GDP by up to 0.9% by 2030, European car, chemical and clean-tech firms may soon stop trying to compete head-on and instead join Chinese supply chains. In Britain, troubled utility Thames Water asked its creditors—including Elliott Management, Silver Point Capital, BlackRock and M&G—to extend the repayment deadline on part of its £20bn debt pile from 2027 to March 2028 as it raises the first £600m of a £2.4bn emergency loan to avoid running out of cash around New Year, leaving Prime Minister Andy Burnham under pressure to choose between a creditor restructuring and special administration. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Technology

Anthropic debuts Claude 5.2 models as Apple rolls out OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro and paid AI packs

Anthropic has launched two upgraded frontier artificial intelligence models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, built to handle complex software migrations, multi-agent orchestration and scientific reasoning faster than September’s 5.1 releases. According to the company, prerelease versions designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in black-hole physics, advanced robotics evaluations and formalised the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours; Fable 5.2 is out immediately, while Mythos 5.2 is restricted to vetted institutions. The launch coincides with Apple’s first move to charge for server-based AI tools: a Monday update to Logic Pro introduces a $49.99 one-time Intelligence Usage Pack for users who exhaust their free allowance, a model set to expand across Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro and iWork this month, even as Apple completed regulatory filings to launch Apple Intelligence on iPads and Macs in China in December and released iOS 27.2.1 and macOS 27.2.1 Golden Gate to fix eMudhra certificate vulnerabilities. (The Verge, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac)

Reviews also arrived on Tuesday for Apple’s first laptop redesign in five years, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, priced from £2,899—a £400 premium over equivalent LCD models amid high memory costs. Sold in 14-inch (1.38kg) and 16-inch (1.82kg) M5 Pro and M5 Max versions, the laptop cuts weight by roughly 15%, restores the glowing Apple lid logo dropped in 2015, and adds the first touchscreen on a Mac, complete with a Dynamic Island around the webcam and a tandem OLED panel reaching 2,000 nits. While reviewers praised the display and touch gestures for iPhone mirroring and photo editing, Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo faces scrutiny after reports blamed hairline cracks along the inner crease of some units on defective display material. Even so, Apple shares closed above $350 on Monday for a record high, days after SEC 10-K disclosures showed that booking overseas profits in Singapore ($2.7bn) and Ireland ($2.6bn) saved Apple $5.3bn compared with the 21% US corporate tax rate in fiscal 2026, despite the OECD’s 15% minimum tax adding $2.5bn to its Singapore bill. (Guardian, MacMagazine, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac)

Palantir lobbied health minister via WhatsApp to bring NHS GP records into its AI platform

Freedom of Information disclosures show that US data firm Palantir privately lobbied former health minister Zubir Ahmed via WhatsApp between July 2025 and March 2026 to extend its artificial intelligence software into NHS family doctor records, despite explicit pledges when its £330m Federated Data Platform contract was signed in 2023 that GP data would stay out of scope. In messages obtained by campaign group Foxglove, Palantir’s UK chief, Louis Mosley, argued that linking primary and secondary care data inside its Foundry software was vital for managing frail patients and urged the minister to get ahead of political opposition from the British Medical Association, the Green Party and Jeremy Corbyn’s Your Party. Although Health Secretary Yvette Cooper told MPs last week that the government sees long-term value in building British sovereign AI when Palantir’s contract reaches a break point in 2029, ministers are expected to extend the deal in the meantime, while the BMA warned that scope creep into GP records risked damaging patient trust. (Guardian)

Take-Two fortifies GTA 6 against AI reverse-engineering as Switch 2 Zelda remake trips up veterans

With ten days left before Rockstar Games launches Grand Theft Auto VI on PlayStation 5 and Xbox on 19 November, parent company Take-Two Interactive has stepped up technical encryption and legal preparations against the threat of artificial intelligence tools being used to decompile console code into unofficial PC ports. After viral episodes last month in which modders made Grand Theft Auto V playable in a browser and hackers released jailbreaks for older PS5 firmware, Anthropic updated Claude to block prompts attempting to reverse-engineer video games; Take-Two chief executive Strauss Zelnick welcomed that move on Monday while warning AI firms to respect third-party copyright. Reaffirming an $8bn to $8.2bn revenue forecast for fiscal 2027, Zelnick noted that anticipation for GTA 6 had prompted rival publishers to crowd into September and caused gamers to hold off on buying other releases, including Take-Two’s NBA 2K27, which sold four million units but missed internal forecasts. Meanwhile, Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has sparked debate by replacing the 1998 Nintendo 64 original’s automatic ledge-jumping with a manual jump button, sending decades of player muscle memory—and Young Link—repeatedly into rivers and boulders. (IGN, IGN, IGN)

Culture

M John Harrison wins Booker Prize at 81 with post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything

M John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for his slim, unsettling novel The End of Everything, becoming at 81 the oldest laureate in the award’s history—surpassing Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019—and the first winner to emerge directly from science fiction. Awarded the £50,000 prize in London on Monday night after a unanimous vote by judges chaired by classicist Mary Beard alongside Jarvis Cocker, Patricia Lockwood, Raymond Antrobus and Rebecca Liu, Harrison prevailed over a shortlist featuring Marlon James, Douglas Stuart, Elizabeth Strout, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry. At 198 pages and published by independent imprint Serpent’s Tail, the novel follows Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie as they muddle through on a near-future Kent coast after an unexplained collapse and the arrival of shape-shifting beings called the iGhetti. (Guardian, BBC)

Born in Warwickshire in 1945, Harrison sold his first story in 1965 and helped shape British speculative fiction at New Worlds magazine in the 1970s, winning the Boardman Tasker prize for Climbers, the Arthur C Clarke Award for Nova Swing and the Goldsmiths Prize for The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again before earning his first Booker nomination this year. He has described The End of Everything as a disaster story in which the catastrophe is humanity’s failure to comprehend a shifting reality, withholding explanation so readers share the characters’ disorientation amid the collapse of rationality in the internet and AI age. Beard praised the book for turning readers upside down while leaving an unexpected trace of optimism, while Booker chief executive Gaby Wood hailed the recognition of a writer who has spent six decades showing that speculative fiction belongs at the centre of literary culture. (Guardian, BBC)

Manchester United edge towards sacking Michael Carrick as City slump and Arsenal’s Ben White returns

Manchester United are moving closer to dismissing head coach Michael Carrick during the November international break after Sunday’s 4-4 draw with Aston Villa left the club 18th in the Premier League and enduring their worst domestic start in 40 years. Having spared Carrick after a 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October on the condition that performances improved across three matches against Chelsea, Roma and Villa, director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada are expected to recommend a change to Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family after seeing United win three of 15 games in all competitions and repeatedly concede early goals. United have sounded out Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann, while USA coach Mauricio Pochettino has a contract clause allowing a move to Old Trafford after next week’s Nations League play-off against Haiti. Across town, Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca is using the break to reassess his high defensive line and lightweight midfield pairing of £125m signing Enzo Fernández and Rayan Cherki after Saturday’s loss at Nottingham Forest condemned City to three straight league defeats following seven opening wins—a sequence last seen in the top flight in 1904—just as the club awaits potential sanctions after being found guilty last month of nearly all of the Premier League’s financial charges. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

In the England camp ahead of this week’s Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain, Arsenal defender Ben White said he held no complaints over the Wembley fans who booed him when he ended his nearly four-year self-imposed international exile against Uruguay earlier this year. White, who left the 2022 World Cup in Qatar for personal reasons and stayed unavailable for the rest of Gareth Southgate’s tenure, was persuaded back by Thomas Tuchel before a knee injury kept him out of last summer’s World Cup. Having made 12 appearances in strong form for Arsenal this term, the 29-year-old said he would never publicly blame anyone over his 2022 exit and was focused on earning a place in Tuchel’s squad for Euro 2028. (Guardian)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

item.title: The Fold — 2026-11-09
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 9 November 2026: Nvidia’s board investigation into Jensen Huang, the opening of COP31 in Turkey, Britain’s shifting green transition rules, Brazil’s Supreme Court inquiry and Apple’s push for an autonomous Siri.
item.content:encoded:
Monday 9 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Nvidia launches an independent board inquiry into chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with an executive suspected of spying for China.
  • World leaders gather in Antalya for the COP31 climate summit as the UN warns that planetary heat accumulation is accelerating.
  • Ministers weigh easing Britain’s 2030 electric vehicle mandate while households face a spring VAT increase on solar panels and heat pumps.
  • Brazil’s Federal Police complete reports on three Supreme Court justices’ ties to the liquidated Banco Master and its former owner.
  • Apple chief executive John Ternus presses software leaders to accelerate work on an autonomous Siri agent for next year.
  • Brighton climb to second in the Premier League behind Arsenal while Manchester United stay in the relegation zone and Crystal Palace prepare to change manager.

News

Nvidia investigates Jensen Huang over suspected Chinese espionage ties

Nvidia’s board of directors has opened an independent investigation into founder and chief executive Jensen Huang following allegations that he became the target of a Chinese intelligence operation through an extramarital affair. In a message sent to employees on Sunday evening, Huang apologised to his wife, children, colleagues and shareholders for his infidelity, accepting full responsibility for his choices while pledging to cooperate with the inquiry. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside legal counsel, will examine his relationship with Huang Le, a Chinese national also known as Alice Huang who served as an executive at the Singapore-based data-centre company Megaspeed. US intelligence officials suspect she was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information on the chipmaker. (Guardian, The Verge, The Verge)

The relationship sits at the intersection of corporate governance and American export controls designed to keep advanced semiconductors out of Chinese hands. Megaspeed has been a major buyer of Nvidia processors and faces a US Commerce Department investigation into whether it helped divert restricted chips to Chinese entities. Photographers captured the two executives drinking whisky together in Taipei in June 2024 and again in May 2025. While Nvidia initially maintained that its chief executive’s contacts with a customer were routine, fresh details emerged on Monday: in early 2025, Alice Huang and business partner Kang Wei pitched investors on a south-east Asian data-centre project worth several hundred million dollars, claiming easy access to graphics chips and citing Alibaba as a client. Earlier this year, short-seller Culper Research alleged that Alibaba secretly funded Megaspeed through shell companies and estimated that over 20% of Nvidia’s fiscal 2026 compute revenue still relied on Chinese demand. (Guardian, BBC)

In Beijing, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun dismissed the espionage claims on Monday as baseless vilification, while state media accused American outlets of manufacturing a spy narrative out of trade disputes. In Washington, the White House struck a forgiving tone. Donald Trump was reportedly briefed on intelligence concerns surrounding Nvidia a year ago and took no action, wary of disrupting a flagship US company or trade talks with China. Speaking on Sunday, the president said he had no regrets, describing Huang as an honourable man and expressing confidence that he would stay in his role. US officials nonetheless worry about whether Huang’s closeness to the administration gave him insights into artificial intelligence policy that could have reached Beijing. (Guardian, The Verge)

For financial markets, the timing is delicate. Valued at roughly $4.5tn (£3.3tn), Nvidia sits at the heart of the global AI build-out, and its shares fell 4.5% in Frankfurt on Monday morning and 5% in US pre-market trading. The drop follows a bruising week in which Wall Street suffered its steepest single-day fall since the pandemic, wiping $3.2tn from market values after US midterm voters backed candidates critical of data-centre energy consumption. Nvidia’s board stated that it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised, and investors including Bill Ackman and Elon Musk stressed Huang’s technical indispensability, though analysts warn that congressional scrutiny and governance risk will linger until the review concludes. (Guardian, Guardian)

COP31 opens in Turkey under a warning of accelerating planetary heat

Diplomats and world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya on Monday for the opening of the UN’s COP31 climate summit, greeted by data showing that heat is building up across Earth’s systems at the fastest pace on record. According to the World Meteorological Organization’s State of the Global Climate update, the global mean surface temperature between January and September 2026 stood at roughly 1.47C above the pre-industrial average. That puts 2026 on course to join 2023, 2024 and 2025 as the four warmest years ever recorded, even though the year began with cooling La Niña conditions in the Pacific. Forecasters warn that a brewing El Niño — projected to be among the strongest in a thousand years — could drive temperatures higher still and intensify heatwaves, droughts and cyclones. (Guardian)

Scientists point to a widening gap between incoming solar energy and the heat escaping back into space. Between 2001 and 2025, that energy imbalance grew at 0.3 watts per square metre each decade, more than double the rate recorded across 1960 to 2025. Atmospheric carbon dioxide reached 426.8 parts per million in 2025, up 53% since 1750 and well above the 356.42 parts per million measured when the UN climate convention was signed in 1992. The oceans, which absorb 90% of excess heat, are marking a tenth straight year of record warmth in their upper 2,000 metres, pushing sea levels to a historic high, while glaciers lost over 400 gigatonnes of ice in a fourth consecutive year of universal retreat across all 19 glacierised regions. (Guardian)

Among the leaders arriving in Antalya is Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whose government hosted last year’s summit in Belém. Lula travelled on Monday with environment minister João Paulo Capobianco, foreign minister Celso Amorim, energy minister Alexandre Silveira, health minister Alexandre Padilha — who is presenting a climate health-financing plan — and development bank chief Aloizio Mercadante. Absent from the delegation were Chamber speaker Hugo Motta and Senate president Davi Alcolumbre, who stayed in Brasília to manage year-end votes and their own leadership races, delaying talks over Lula’s fourth-term cabinet reshuffle until he returns from the Asean summit in Manila on 16 November. (Folha, Folha)

Ministers weigh softer electric vehicle rules as households face a spring green-tech tax rise

As British ministers head to Turkey for the climate talks, the government’s domestic net-zero policies face strain on two fronts. Whitehall is expected this week to reduce the zero-emission vehicle mandate, which requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be electric by 2030 ahead of a 2035 phase-out of new petrol and diesel models. Prime minister Andy Burnham has recused himself from the decision because of his wife’s links to an electric vehicle firm, leaving Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh to chair the key meetings. While carmakers have pleaded for relief, environmental groups and Energy UK warn that softening the 2030 target — shortly after approval of the Jackdaw North Sea gas field — threatens the investment certainty needed for charging infrastructure. (BBC)

Households trying to cut their reliance on fossil fuels also face a steep tax rise in the spring. Ministers are resisting pressure to cancel the expiry on 1 April of the 5% VAT exemption on domestic heat pumps, solar panels and home batteries, a move that could add up to £1,530 to a combined smart home installation. Demand for upgrades has hit record highs since the Middle East conflict caused European gas prices to double, yet the Budget signalled cuts to total heat-pump grant funding alongside the return of VAT. With domestic electricity bills zero-rated until July next year, trade bodies Solar Energy UK and the Heat Pump Association warn that the April cliff-edge will trigger a winter rush for installers and perversely tax families more heavily for saving energy than for consuming it. (Guardian)

Federal Police reports examine Brazilian Supreme Court justices’ ties to Banco Master

Brazil’s Federal Police have completed three reports examining the ties between Supreme Court justices Alexandre de Moraes, Dias Toffoli and Kassio Nunes Marques and banker Daniel Vorcaro, former owner of the liquidated Banco Master. Requested by court president Edson Fachin, the documents set out contacts with potential criminal implications without making formal charges and will go to Fachin this week. Phone records show that before Vorcaro’s arrest on 17 November 2025 over suspected billion-real frauds, he flew by private jet to Brasília on 14 and 16 November to meet Moraes at his residence, sent disappearing WhatsApp screenshots, and asked the justice to help delay police operations. Returning to São Paulo on the Sunday evening, Vorcaro searched Google for the Tremembé prison and the Brasília judge who ordered his arrest the next day. Amid the fallout, the two police commissioners leading the Master inquiry are being removed in a departmental reorganisation, while justices are backing Davi Alcolumbre’s Senate re-election to keep impeachment petitions in check. Separately on Monday, Justice Luiz Fux suspended the two-year removal imposed by the National Council of Justice on former Lava Jato judge Gabriela Hardt. (Canal Meio, Folha, Folha)

The banking scandal shaped President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s first national broadcast since winning a fourth term. Speaking on Sunday night, Lula argued that the judiciary needs impartial, ethical magistrates free from conflicts of interest and personal enrichment projects. Seeking to calm financial markets, he reversed his campaign dismissal of fiscal surpluses, saying public debt and high interest rates worry him and pledging to respect fiscal rules and lift investment above 20% of GDP, though he announced no specific spending cuts. Lula also accused big tech companies of amplifying election disinformation and aimed a barb at defeated rival Flávio Bolsonaro — who left for the US after missing a passport surrender deadline — by saying he had never abandoned his country. New Quaest polling shows 62% of Brazilians aware of Flávio’s trip think he was wrong to leave and 56% believe he fled to evade justice, while 28% of voters now say they would disapprove of their child marrying a political rival, up ten points in a year. (Folha, Canal Meio, Folha)

Prosecutors seek up to 15 years in prison as Russell Brand is sentenced

Prosecutors at Southwark Crown Court called on Monday for Russell Brand to serve a category-one sentence of 10 to 15 years after the 51-year-old former comedian was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women between 2004 and 2009. Chief prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC told Mr Justice Bennathan that Brand used his fame and influence to access women and fostered a culture of impunity around himself, describing how the rape of a 21-year-old woman at his home left her with severe trauma that ended her comedy ambitions. Defence barrister Ian Winter KC asked for mercy, arguing the offences were isolated incidents committed 17 years ago before Brand changed his life and warning of the impact on his wife and three young children. (Guardian)

Victim impact statements read in court highlighted the workplace tolerance that protected Brand at the peak of his broadcasting career. One woman assaulted in a Channel 4 radio studio said senior management brushed her immediate complaint under the carpet, while another woman attacked at Capital Radio’s offices in 2009 described flinching at his voice for two decades. Publishers Pan Macmillan and Hodder & Stoughton have withdrawn Brand’s books from sale, and Metropolitan Police detectives leading Operation Actinolite confirmed they have sent files on two more complainants to prosecutors while investigating allegations from at least ten further women, including a then 16-year-old girl. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Kraków gunman dies in hospital as EU sues border contractors and fog blankets Britain

A 24-year-old Polish gunman who killed six people in Kraków’s Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon, as well as his parents and sister at their home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, died in hospital early on Monday from wounds suffered in a shootout with police. Wearing military-style gear and a bulletproof vest, the attacker drove into the crowded square and opened fire at random before officers Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański shot him within three minutes; four Polish citizens, a 32-year-old British man and a 51-year-old Austrian woman were killed and 16 people injured. Police found two AR-15 rifles, two handguns and hundreds of rounds in his car, and counter-terrorism prosecutors are examining extremist emblems on his clothing after interior minister Marcin Kierwiński linked him to radical far-right views. (Guardian, BBC)

Closer to home, dense radiation fog reduced visibility below 50 metres across swathes of England, eastern Wales and Northern Ireland on Monday, disrupting flights at Heathrow and closing part of the southbound M40 after weekend mist contributed to a 30-vehicle pile-up on the M20 in Kent and a 19-car crash on the A303 in Hampshire; a fresh Met Office yellow warning runs from Monday evening until Tuesday morning. Travellers crossing into continental Europe have also faced three-hour queues at Schengen borders, and newly disclosed accounts reveal that the EU’s IT agency, EU-Lisa, has sued consortium partners IBM, French IT firm Atos and Italian contractor Leonardo in an Estonian court over development delays to the error-plagued biometric Entry/Exit System launched in October 2025. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

Technology

Apple chief John Ternus presses software teams to turn Siri into an autonomous agent

Months after succeeding Tim Cook as Apple’s chief executive, John Ternus is pressing software chief Craig Federighi to speed up the company’s artificial intelligence roadmap and turn Siri into an autonomous agent able to rival OpenAI’s Dots, Meta’s Muse and Grok. In a recent closed-door meeting, Ternus urged Federighi to move quickly beyond the request-based Siri AI introduced in iOS 27, amid internal frustration over Federighi’s cautious, debate-heavy style and 12-to-18-month planning horizon. The push comes as Mike Rockwell, the Vision Pro creator who rescued Siri’s engineering after its earlier two-year delay, weighs stepping down next year, and as Apple restructures its iOS 28 (Bell) and macOS 28 (Poppy) development milestones to give engineers six weeks of coding and two weeks of integration per phase. (The Verge, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine)

Early steps toward that goal are arriving in the iOS 27.3 developer preview. Removing the initial restriction to narrow domains like calendars and messages, Apple will let any app expose up to 40 App Intents as natural-language tools via Private Cloud Compute, alongside Markdown “skills” that chain up to 32 actions across apps; deeper control of Apple’s own apps ships in January, with third-party integrations due in spring, while watchOS 27.3 adds encrypted on-device Siri Recap meeting notes. Elsewhere in the ecosystem, macOS 27.3 tightens Full Disk Access rules after rogue AI agents tapped into iMessage databases, the foldable iPhone Duo has passed 100,000 optimised App Store titles, and Apple has dropped a 40% retail staff target for free-trial sign-ups and required customers to tap the acceptance button themselves after consumer advocate Louis Rossmann exposed unconsented subscriptions. (MacStories, 9to5Mac, MacStories, 9to5Mac)

Meta takes Instagram’s AI age checks global while Suno faces lawsuits over Elvis and Eminem

Meta is rolling out its artificial-intelligence age-estimation tools worldwide on Instagram to identify teenagers who registered with false adult birthdates and move millions more into protected Teen Accounts. Following an August legal settlement worth $17.1bn and earlier launches in the US, EU and Brazil, the system scans interaction patterns, birthday posts and visual cues such as height and bone structure in uploaded videos — plus Apple’s age-range signal in Australia — to remove children under 13 and place 13-to-17-year-olds under default privacy and messaging limits, with US parents receiving explanatory notifications this month. Meanwhile, AI music generator Suno faces two new lawsuits from Elvis Presley rights holders and the publisher of Eminem’s catalogue, who invoke Tennessee’s ELVIS Act against voice cloning to accuse the company of mechanically replicating the artists’ voices and lyrics without a licence. (The Verge, 9to5Mac, The Verge)

Culture

Grand Theft Auto VI takes over Oxford Street as gaming’s flagship series nears launch

Ten days before Grand Theft Auto VI launches on 19 November, Rockstar Games has staged its first British retail takeover on the ground floor of Selfridges on Oxford Street, parking a blue Grotti Cheetah Classic in the window and drawing online queues past 100,000 for Vice City merchandise including a sold-out £2,500 varsity jacket. Console preloads going live in New Zealand on Monday revealed an install size of up to 212GB — including 22GB of audio — alongside PlayStation 5 Pro ray-tracing enhancements, capping a trajectory that began with DMA Design’s 1997 top-down original in Scotland and grew through 230m sales of Grand Theft Auto V into a sequel costing over $1bn. Meanwhile, members of the original Mass Effect voice cast united for an N7 Day video appeal and billboard campaign urging fans to help save the franchise weeks after Electronic Arts shut down BioWare and cancelled Mass Effect 5. (IGN, IGN, Guardian, IGN)

Coventry Cathedral’s medieval glass goes online ahead of tonight’s Booker Prize

Thousands of 15th-century stained-glass fragments by master glazier John Thornton, packed into 30 crates in a cellar after the Luftwaffe bombed Coventry Cathedral in 1940, have been catalogued with World Monuments Fund support and placed on digital display for the first time in nearly 90 years. In London tonight, judging chair Dame Mary Beard and panel members Jarvis Cocker, Patricia Lockwood, Raymond Antrobus and Rebecca Liu will award the £50,000 Booker Prize, with past winners Marlon James (The Disappearers) and Douglas Stuart (John of John) facing Elizabeth Strout, M John Harrison, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry. In music, U2 have released Carnaval de Luz, their first album of new songs in nearly a decade, featuring a returning Larry Mullen Jr and a closing duet with the late Dolly Parton, while in Brazil researcher Gabriel Gonzaga has uncovered 12 unrecorded early-1950s compositions and 17 arrangements by Tom Jobim ahead of the composer’s 2027 centenary. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Canal Meio)

Sports

Brighton close in on leaders Arsenal as Manchester United and Crystal Palace hit crisis

Arsenal enter the November international break six points clear of Manchester City at the top of the Premier League after a 1-0 win over Hull, though a return of 15 goals from 10 games has prompted Mikel Arteta to call for more chaos and ruthlessness in the first half against low blocks. Fabian Hürzeler’s Brighton moved into second place as Arsenal’s closest challengers with a commanding 2-0 home win over 10-man Brentford, sealed by another long-range strike from Paraguayan midfielder Diego Gómez and a Pascal Gross penalty after Igor Thiago’s VAR red card. In the Women’s Super League, Alessia Russo’s first-half double — her seventh goal in four games — gave Renée Slegers’s Arsenal a vital 2-1 victory away to Liverpool ahead of their trip to face Barcelona. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

At the bottom of the men’s top flight, Crystal Palace are poised to sack Pierre Sage on Monday after a 3-1 loss to Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool left them bottom for the first time since December 2017 with 24 goals conceded in 10 games, making former Spurs and Brentford boss Thomas Frank the favourite to succeed him ahead of Sean Dyche and Vítor Pereira. Manchester United sit 18th on eight points after a club-record eighth league game without a win, needing stoppage-time goals from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu to salvage a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa after mistakes by Senne Lammens, Diogo Dalot and Leny Yoro, leaving Michael Carrick to brush off resignation talk. Elsewhere, Enzo Le Fée’s penalty gave Sunderland a 1-0 win over Chelsea to climb off the foot of the table, Evanilson’s strike in a fifth straight league game helped Bournemouth beat Ipswich 2-1 for a club-record-equalling eighth consecutive win, Nottingham Forest beat Manchester City 3-1 and Leeds edged Tottenham 1-0. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 28 October 2026: Israel’s election deadlock, Brazil’s post-election uncertainty, Britain’s Budget preparations and Apple’s new Macs.
item.content:encoded:
Wednesday 28 October 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Israel’s exit polls leave both main blocs short of a majority.
  • Flávio Bolsonaro’s reported departure follows a passport surrender deadline.
  • UK and EU officials prepare discussions before November’s summit.
  • The Budget is expected to focus on household costs and devolution.
  • Apple announces M6 versions of the iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro.
  • Fleetwood eliminate Arsenal from the Carabao Cup on penalties.

News

Israel’s election leaves coalition talks on a new footing

Israel’s election produced no clear route to a parliamentary majority in Tuesday’s exit polls, leaving Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing coalition and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc facing difficult negotiations. The projections put the two camps level, with neither reaching the 61 seats needed to control the 120-seat Knesset. Likud could still emerge as the largest individual party. These were estimates as counting continued, and the eventual distribution of seats will determine who can credibly assemble a government. (Guardian)

The biggest projected change was a sharp increase in representation for Palestinian parties, from ten seats to around 17 or 18. That gives Arab Israeli leaders potential influence over whether the opposition can replace Netanyahu. Eisenkot and his partners would need to negotiate with Ra’am, the United Arab List, and possibly the Joint List. Ra’am’s leader, Mansour Abbas, has experience of joining a governing coalition, having participated in Naftali Bennett’s administration. Tuesday’s projections suggested his party alone might lack the seats to deliver a majority to Eisenkot’s bloc. (Guardian)

Talks with the Joint List would bring harder disagreements into the open. Eisenkot has set conditions involving Israel’s identity as a Jewish and democratic state, the principles of its declaration of independence, military conscription for Palestinian Israeli citizens and condemnation of Hamas. Hadash, the largest faction within the Joint List, rejected the premise that the opposition could dictate the terms. Those differences concern the place of Arab citizens in the state and the obligations expected of them. Resolving them would require substantial political commitments from parties whose cooperation has clear parliamentary value. (Guardian)

If the results confirm the deadlock, President Isaac Herzog will have discretion over whom to invite to try to form a government. Netanyahu’s administration would remain in a caretaker role during negotiations. An opposition minority government supported through individual agreements is another possibility, though it would face an uncertain life in parliament. The result therefore leaves several stages between election night and a change of leadership. Arab parties’ gains could make that change possible, while the difficulty of reaching an agreement gives Netanyahu time to seek another route to power. (Guardian)

Flávio Bolsonaro’s departure deepens Brazil’s political uncertainty

Flávio Bolsonaro was reported to have left Brazil for the United States on Tuesday after losing the presidential election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The senator missed a morning deadline to surrender his passport to federal police. His whereabouts and route became the subject of conflicting accounts, including reports of travel through Argentina. Allies described plans to seek asylum in the US, and the US State Department indicated that he and his family would receive visas allowing entry. The details of his movements remained unsettled in Tuesday’s coverage. (Guardian)

The passport order arose from a criminal investigation into possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme connected to betting companies. An investigation does not establish guilt. Bolsonaro had denied intending to leave Brazil in a video posted on Monday, and had yet to concede his election defeat. Lawmakers from Lula’s Workers’ party asked the supreme court to order his arrest and sought an Interpol red notice. Those requests were further steps sought by political opponents, rather than evidence that an international arrest alert had already been issued. (Guardian)

His departure adds a leadership question to the right’s electoral defeat. Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest over an attempted coup, while Eduardo Bolsonaro is already in the US. São Paulo governor Tarcísio de Freitas is among the figures positioned to gain influence as the family’s role becomes more uncertain. Lula condemned Flávio’s apparent flight during celebrations of his 81st birthday. For the re-elected president, the immediate task is to prepare another administration while legal proceedings and the defeated candidate’s response continue to shape the political atmosphere. (Guardian)

UK–EU talks reopen the question of a closer relationship

British and European officials are expected to discuss options for the future relationship before the UK–EU summit on 20 November, with freedom of movement entering the political debate. Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds indicated that officials would consider the longer-term possibilities. Downing Street stressed that the immediate work concerns agreements already being prepared within Labour’s manifesto commitments, and a government spokesperson denied that current discussions covered freedom of movement. The difference in emphasis leaves the scope and timing of any wider negotiations unclear. (BBC)

Prime minister Andy Burnham has called for an open discussion of the relationship, while maintaining that major changes would need a general-election mandate. Labour’s 2024 programme ruled out returning to free movement, the single market or a customs union during this parliament, which must end by 2029. Free movement allows EU citizens to live, work and study across member countries and is a condition of single-market membership. Any attempt to pursue that deeper relationship would therefore involve choices about migration alongside trade and economic rules. (BBC)

For the coming summit, the practical agenda includes food and drink, electricity, emissions trading and youth mobility. Those areas offer a nearer-term test of what closer cooperation can deliver. Within Labour, MPs representing Brexit-supporting constituencies have warned that reopening the broader argument could damage trust. Burnham has also left questions over a possible referendum unresolved, with Downing Street saying no decision has been made. Businesses and citizens will need to distinguish the agreements being pursued now from options that would require another electoral mandate and further negotiation. (BBC)

Economy

The Budget tests the government’s room to act

John Healey enters Wednesday’s Budget facing a difficult combination of rising energy costs, pressure on household finances and limited scope for additional public spending. Expectations on Tuesday centred on targeted help with the cost of living, particularly for vulnerable households. Banks were preparing for a possible levy or surcharge to help finance support. The chancellor has promised longer-term action on energy costs, but the detailed measures and their funding will become clear when he presents the Budget. Advance indications remain proposals until the formal announcements. (BBC)

The government also intends to move more powers and resources to local leaders, making devolution a central part of its economic programme. That raises practical questions about how local spending will be scrutinised and how responsibilities will be shared with Whitehall. Further defence investment is expected, while the full route to spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030 is due in next year’s spending review. Several large commitments therefore stretch beyond a single fiscal statement and will depend on decisions still to come. (BBC)

There are some stronger signals in growth, productivity and employment, yet the Middle East conflict has renewed pressure on energy prices and borrowing costs. Labour’s commitment to avoid increases in income tax, national insurance and VAT further limits the choices available. Healey must explain how immediate support fits within those constraints and the prime minister’s wider promises of change. The sums, eligibility rules and implementation dates will determine how much of the Budget households actually feel over the winter. (BBC)

Rosebank exposes a divide over climate accounting

A cabinet disagreement over the Rosebank oilfield is turning on how Britain accounts for emissions and weighs the benefits of new North Sea production. Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has been leaning towards rejecting the development, while chancellor John Healey favours approval. Supporters argue that the field could operate within the UK’s domestic carbon budgets because much of its oil would be exported. Emissions from burning that oil overseas would then appear in other countries’ accounts, even though the climate consequences extend across borders. (Guardian)

The distinction matters to the approval process. Ministers must consider emissions associated with using the fuel, following the legal challenge to the earlier environmental consent. Taking those emissions into account and assigning them to a domestic carbon budget are separate parts of the assessment. Climate campaigners argue that allowing another major field would undermine the transition away from fossil fuels. Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth have urged the prime minister to consider the cumulative effect of decisions on drilling, airport expansion and support for lower-carbon heating. (Guardian)

The Treasury has a financial interest too: expected tax receipts from Rosebank have already been incorporated into its calculations. The operator estimates revenues for the government could reach £500m a year by the end of this parliament. Rejecting the project would leave ministers to address the resulting gap. The energy department says the decision will follow the regulatory process and consider environmental assessments and public representations. Approval remains unresolved, with jobs, investment, energy security and climate commitments all part of the argument. (Guardian)

Technology

Apple refreshes the iMac and entry-level MacBook Pro

Apple introduced an M6 version of its entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro on Tuesday, retaining the existing design while changing the hardware inside. The US starting price is $1,999, with 16GB of unified memory and 1TB of storage. Buyers can configure up to 32GB of memory and 4TB of storage. The display remains Liquid Retina XDR, with an optional nano-texture finish. Pre-orders open on 28 October, and deliveries are scheduled to begin on 6 November. (MacStories)

Connectivity includes Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, MagSafe, an SDXC card slot and a headphone socket. Apple claims up to 24 hours of battery life, with faster charging available through its 96W adapter rather than the 70W unit supplied. The company also claims graphics and on-device AI improvements over the M5 model. Those are manufacturer figures; the size of any benefit in everyday use will depend on the software, workload and configuration. Memory bandwidth also varies between the base model and the higher-memory versions. (MacStories)

The iMac’s update brings M6 and faster connections

The iMac moves from M4 to M6, starting at $1,499 in the US, with pre-orders opening on 28 October and deliveries from 6 November. Apple is offering two chip configurations, alongside memory starting at 16GB. The higher specification can be equipped with 32GB of memory, up to 2TB of storage and optional 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet. Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 are included, while the number of Thunderbolt 4 ports depends on the model. (MacStories)

The familiar all-in-one format remains, with a 4.5K display, a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and a colour-matched keyboard. The updated machine can drive two external 6K displays. Apple’s performance comparisons include much older Intel and M1 models as well as the M4 generation, so the reference machine matters when reading the headline claims. Households and workplaces replacing older desktops will be looking at a different scale of improvement from owners of a recent iMac. Independent testing will help establish where the new hardware delivers its biggest gains. (MacStories)

Creator Studio adds editing tools and AI assistants

Apple’s creative and productivity software will receive a substantial update in November, bringing MotionVFX tools into Final Cut Pro and Motion after Apple’s acquisition of the plug-in maker in March. Final Cut Pro will gain templates, graphics, titles, transitions and tools for tasks including tracking and colour grading. Closer integration with Pixelmator Pro will allow images in a video timeline to be edited without a separate export and import cycle. Caption transcription will expand to another 23 languages. (MacStories)

Pixelmator Pro will gain generative fill, while Logic Pro will receive an updated interface, expanded stem separation and a beta assistant. Keynote, Pages and Numbers will also add beta assistants using Apple and OpenAI models. On the Mac, support for the Model Context Protocol will let external AI agents connect to those productivity apps. A JSON-based interchange format for Keynote is intended to make presentations more accessible to automated workflows. Existing Creator Studio subscribers will receive the additions as they roll out, with a further Freeform and Pixelmator integration planned for December. (MacStories)

Fake responses swamped the disposable-vape consultation

More than three-quarters of the responses to the government’s 2023 tobacco and vapes consultation were identified as automated, according to research published on Tuesday. Health officials classified 90,835 of 118,756 submissions as bot-generated and excluded them from decision-making. Almost all of those automated entries opposed the proposed ban on disposable vapes. Many were duplicated and arrived rapidly from a small number of internet addresses, providing signals that helped officials detect the interference. (Guardian)

The study, by health-policy researchers at Edinburgh and Bath and published in Tobacco Control, describes an attempt to distort a formal public-health consultation at considerable scale. The ban subsequently became law. The findings do not establish who organised the campaign, and concerns about commercial influence should be kept separate from proof of responsibility. The health department says its controls worked in this case. Researchers warn that improving systems may make future campaigns harder to identify. For public bodies, the challenge is to preserve participation by real people while preventing repeated machine-generated submissions from creating a false impression of public opinion. (Guardian)

Digital landlines face a resilience test

MPs have warned that the move to internet-based landlines could leave people in remote communities unable to call for help during power cuts. Operators aim to complete the change by the end of January. Traditional analogue phones can continue to operate using power from the telephone network; digital services depend on equipment such as a home router, which needs its own electricity supply. Where mobile coverage is weak, losing that connection can remove the remaining way to raise an alarm. (BBC)

Representatives from the Western Isles, the West Country and the Lake District questioned whether the backup arrangements are sufficient for prolonged storms. Battery units supplied to vulnerable customers can keep equipment working for an hour or more, but outages can last considerably longer, and mobile masts may fail too. Security minister Dan Jarvis promised to examine the concerns and raise them with the relevant department. The government says the ageing analogue network is becoming less reliable and that vulnerable customers, including telecare users, must receive free backup batteries. The practical issue is whether each household’s arrangements last through the emergencies it is likely to encounter. (BBC)

A possible hinge fault comes into focus on the iPhone Duo

A teardown assessment has identified a possible explanation for broken inner screens on some newly released iPhone Duo handsets. iFixit’s lead teardown technician, Shahram Mokhtari, points to a place where the flexible display may press against part of the hinge. The central support structure needs to move as the phone closes, allowing the screen room to bend. If it fails to drop sufficiently, contact could concentrate stress at one point. Images of damaged devices have shown a dark spot and lines near that area. (The Verge)

Apple acknowledged a problem on Monday and is replacing affected units. It describes the number as small, but has not disclosed enough data to establish a failure rate. The proposed mechanism remains an expert assessment rather than a confirmed explanation for every damaged phone. Foldable screens and hinges contain delicate components, and individual failures do not by themselves establish how widespread a design problem is. Replacement experience and evidence from more devices will be needed to determine the scale of the issue. Apple has not announced a recall. (The Verge)

Sports

Fleetwood knock Arsenal out on penalties

Arsenal were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by League Two Fleetwood Town after a 1–1 draw and a penalty shootout at Highbury. Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave the hosts the lead, holding off Marli Salmon before finishing past Illan Meslier. Viktor Gyökeres equalised after the interval, but Arsenal could not turn their greater control into a winner. Fleetwood goalkeeper Jay Lynch saved Bruno Guimarães’ penalty, and Conor Haughey converted the decisive kick to send the hosts into the quarter-finals. (Guardian)

The evening brought interruptions and disciplinary trouble as well as an upset. A drone above the pitch caused an early delay, and Max Dowman was sent off after reacting to Harrison Neal. Martin Ødegaard’s introduction improved Arsenal’s play after a poor first half, while Lynch made important late saves from Ben White and Gyökeres to preserve the draw. For Fleetwood manager Matt Lawlor, who was not managing a year ago, the result is a landmark. For Arsenal, a rotated side’s difficult night ended with one route to a trophy closed. (Guardian)

Carrick stays for United’s trip to Chelsea

Manchester United have decided Michael Carrick will remain in charge for Saturday’s visit to Chelsea after defeats at Como and at home to Bournemouth intensified scrutiny of his position. United are 16th in the Premier League, with a Champions League match against Roma and a league game against Aston Villa to follow before the international break. The club has set no public deadline for a turnaround. (BBC)

The problems extend across the squad and its relationship with the coaching staff. Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned the tactics after the European defeat and was subsequently on the bench against Bournemouth. Senior figures believe the players are performing below their capabilities, while recruitment and the work of the football leadership have also come under examination. Keeping Carrick gives him another opportunity to change results, but the immediate schedule leaves little breathing room. Stamford Bridge will provide the first test of whether the same group can begin to recover. (BBC)
